parts.title: Types of sequence change
paragraphs: A substitution replaces one nucleotide with another. An insertion adds nucleotide sequence, while a deletion removes sequence. The effect depends on where the change occurs and which biological process uses that region. A change within a protein-coding region must be interpreted relative to a stated reading frame. Changes in regulatory or RNA-processing regions require a different kind of prediction.

An insertion or deletion whose length is not a multiple of three can shift the downstream reading frame within a coding region. This frameshift changes how later bases are grouped into codons and may alter later amino acids or stop placement. A three-base insertion preserves the downstream frame, although it can add amino-acid information and affect a codon at the insertion boundary.

Write the original and changed sequence with aligned positions before translating. For coding DNA ATGGAATTTTAA, a single added A after ATG gives ATGAGAATTTTAA. In the first-base frame, the later triplets differ from the reference. This prediction assumes the segment lies in a translated region with the stated frame. A one-base change outside that region is not automatically a protein frameshift.

parts.title: Effects on gene products
paragraphs: A synonymous, or silent, substitution leaves the encoded amino acid unchanged in the stated frame. For example, RNA GAA and GAG both specify glutamate in the standard code. A missense substitution changes the amino acid, while a nonsense substitution creates a premature stop codon. These terms describe immediate coding consequences; they do not independently establish an organism's full phenotype.

A regulatory mutation can change when, where or how strongly a gene is expressed without changing its encoded amino-acid sequence. A change at a splice boundary can alter the mature transcript. Even a synonymous substitution may have RNA-related effects in some contexts. Therefore, no amino-acid change means no change to that predicted sequence, rather than proof of no possible biological effect anywhere.

Effects can be harmful, neutral or beneficial under specific conditions. Compare the changed sequence with RNA, protein and functional evidence. If the measurements show no difference under tested conditions, report no detected effect in that assay. If a shortened product is predicted, test whether it is produced and functional. The strength of the conclusion depends on the level of evidence, not simply on the mutation category.

parts.title: Inheritance and variation
paragraphs: A somatic mutation occurs in a body-cell lineage. As that cell divides, daughter cells may receive the change. A mutation confined to body tissue usually does not pass to offspring through gametes. A germ-line mutation occurs in cells that contribute to gametes, so it may pass to offspring. Before predicting inheritance, identify the cell lineage where the change occurred.

Mutation can create a new allele sequence. Recombination usually puts existing sequence variants into new combinations during meiosis. Errors in chromosome processes can also create changes, but rearranging existing alleles is not the same as making a new allele at every locus. Compare the sequence itself with the combination inherited from the parents. They describe different sources of variation.

Mutations do not arise because an organism knows it will need a trait. Their origin is not directed toward a future benefit. Later, selection can change how common an inherited variant becomes. This can happen when the variant affects reproductive success in that environment. Separate the two questions: how did a variant arise, and why did its frequency change? Unit D uses counts, inheritance and environmental evidence to study the second question.

parts.title: Evaluating mutation evidence
paragraphs: A mutagen is an agent that can increase the frequency of genetic changes under specified conditions. Dose, exposure route, duration, biological system and the measured endpoint all affect explanation. A controlled comparison should include a reference condition and use the same detection method. An association between exposure and a change does not by itself identify the exact molecular mechanism.

Consider a variant found repeatedly in tumour samples. Recurrence alone can suggest a research question, but functional evidence strengthens a proposed role. If the variant changes a growth pathway in cells and reducing that activity changes growth in matched models, the observations converge on a possible mechanism. The result still has a scope: tumour context, other variants and model limitations matter.

Communicate evidence in layers: sequence change, RNA or protein effect, cell behaviour and broader outcome. Name uncertainty at each transition. A mutation presentation should include sources and types, specific sequence examples, effects, inheritance routes and a misconception correction. Use fictional sequences and supplied data for the classroom task. Neither an exposure model nor a tumour example provides a diagnosis or treatment decision for an individual.

parts.title: Cutting and joining DNA
paragraphs: Restriction enzymes recognize specific DNA sequences and cut the backbone at characteristic positions. A recognition site is the sequence pattern associated with an enzyme's action. Some cuts produce short single-stranded overhangs, called sticky ends, while others produce blunt ends. The resulting fragments depend on where the recognition sites occur in the original DNA, so the source sequence constrains the products.

Compatible sticky ends can pair through complementary bases, bringing fragments into an arrangement suitable for joining. DNA ligase then seals suitable breaks in the sugar–phosphate backbone. Pairing and joining are different steps: base interactions align the ends, while ligase forms a covalent connection. Ligase does not invent the required base sequence or make every unrelated end immediately compatible.

For a recombinant-DNA plan, specify the DNA source, recognition sites, intended insert and receiving molecule. Predict the fragments before describing a successful construct. Cutting with a familiar enzyme name is not proof that the intended gene was isolated. A later sequence or fragment check is needed to confirm the product. The most useful diagram shows the original, the cut ends and the verified joined arrangement.

parts.title: Transforming cells
paragraphs: A vector is a DNA vehicle used to carry selected genetic material into a cell or maintain it there. A plasmid is a DNA molecule that can replicate separately from the main chromosome in a suitable host. A recombinant plasmid may contain an insert, a selectable feature and sequences needed for its intended expression. Each element serves a different purpose in the experimental design.

Transformation is uptake of external genetic material by a cell in the context used here. Uptake does not guarantee that every cell receives the intended construct or expresses the inserted gene. Selection identifies cells with a feature linked to survival or detection under specified conditions. A surviving colony can contain a vector without the desired insert, so selection must be followed by suitable verification.

Check insert presence, orientation, sequence and expression separately. A failed insert-specific PCR result is consistent with an absent insert but can also reflect a failed assay; controls are needed. A plasmid's presence does not mean it necessarily integrated into the host chromosome. Some constructs remain separate, while stable integration requires its own mechanism and evidence. Trace each claim from uptake through persistence and expression before concluding that a cell's function changed as intended.

parts.title: Amplifying and separating
paragraphs: PCR stands for polymerase chain reaction. It makes many copies of a selected DNA region. Follow one temperature cycle: the strands separate, primers bind to matching sites, and a heat-tolerant polymerase extends them. Repeat the cycle to make more copies. The primer positions help define the target region. Detecting a signal depends both on that target being present and on the method working under the chosen conditions.

Gel electrophoresis uses an electric field to separate DNA or RNA fragments. In the standard DNA comparison here, smaller fragments usually travel farther through the gel. A ladder of known fragment sizes helps estimate the sample's sizes. A band contains many molecules that moved about the same distance. It gives size evidence, but it does not reveal every base in those molecules.

Compare the controls before interpreting a sample. A negative control checks for contamination or copying where none is expected. A known positive control checks that the method can produce the expected signal. A band in the negative control makes sample bands harder to trust. Also check the gel's resolution. An ordinary gel may not clearly separate fragments just one base apart. Report what the bands show before claiming a sequence change or identity.

parts.title: Genetic evidence and relatedness
paragraphs: DNA can help test relatedness when matching regions are compared. Alignment places corresponding positions together. Greater similarity may support a closer relationship under the chosen model. The result also depends on the region, its rate of change and the sample. A short sequence match is not proof that two whole genomes are identical or that only one relationship is possible.

Nuclear DNA usually includes contributions from both parents in a sexual cross. Human mitochondrial DNA is passed mainly through the maternal line. Chloroplast DNA comes from a plant organelle; its inheritance varies by species and is often from one parent. These sources can record different histories. State which was sampled instead of treating all DNA as one interchangeable measure.

The supplied investigation gives both a short coding segment and separate measurements of larger fragments. Reference and substitution models have lengths 400+600 bases; the insertion model has 401+600. An ordinary gel may not resolve that one-base change. Use oriented sequences to identify the precise change. Do not derive the full fragment lengths from the short excerpt or treat a size match as complete sequence identity.

For a source comparison, matching one DNA marker can leave many possible sources. Comparing additional informative, independent markers can improve discrimination. Check the method with suitable controls and consider related samples that may share alleles. More markers do not turn one band into a whole-genome match; the strength of the inference depends on the combined evidence and its quality.

parts.title: Applications and uncertainty
paragraphs: Genetic tools can support research, testing, farming and conservation. Gene therapy aims to alter genetic function in a treatment setting. Genetic testing measures selected features for a stated question. Success at one molecular step does not prove that the whole plan worked. Uptake, expression, function and delivery each need evidence. Wider effects also need to be checked.

A technology can have intended and unintended effects on people and the environment. A crop construct may meet a farming goal while raising questions about costs, access or ecological effects. A matching sequence in another plant does not prove one transfer route. Research for a sustainable society, economy and environment must test benefits and risks under the actual conditions of use.

In the supplied investigation, predict how an insertion and a substitution affect the coding segment and the larger fragments. Record both kinds of evidence and compare what each can resolve. Propose controls and another test. Revise the claim that matching bands prove identical DNA. For a fictional decision, also consider consent, privacy, equity and a contrasting view. Explain the supported benefit and what remains uncertain.
